h1: Fermenting a lager-style beer without a fridge in a warm country
title: Lager-Style Beer Without a Fridge | Craft Beer School
desc: True lagers want 8 to 13 °C. Here are honest ways to make a crisp, clean lager-style beer in a warm country with no temperature control.
teaser: A real lager needs cold. A good lager-style beer needs less than you think, if you pick the yeast and process with care.
standfirst: Without a fridge you cannot make a classic lager. You can make a clean, crisp beer in the same spirit, using the right yeast, a careful process and cheap cooling tricks.
sections: Lager yeast ferments best around 8 to 13 °C and is then matured cold for weeks. The cold holds back esters, so the beer tastes clean. That is physics and biology. No trick fully replaces it. If you cannot hold those temperatures, the honest answer is to make a different beer in the lager style rather than pretend.
Option one: a clean ale yeast

A well-behaved ale yeast such as a Kölsch strain ferments cleanly at 16 to 19 °C and is lager-like if fed good wort. Kölsch is itself a hybrid style. Pair it with pilsner malt, a modest hop addition and cool conditioning. This is the nearest thing to lager in a country with mild winter nights.
Option two: a lager yeast fermented warm

Some dry lager strains tolerate the high teens °C and produce fewer off-notes than you would expect, in the way that California common beer (steam beer) does. Expect a little more fruitiness than a true lager. Pitch a generous amount, at least double a normal ale pitch, because stressed yeast makes the worst flavours. Aerate well.

Some kveik strains ferment so cleanly, even in the high 20s °C, that brewers have used them for lager-style beers. The beer finishes in a few days and is crisp enough for a hot day. See choosing yeast for a warm room. It will not match a Czech pilsner, but it is cleaner than most would guess.
Make the most of cheap cold

If you can reach 16 to 18 °C using a water bath, a wet towel and a fan, or frozen bottles, hold it there for the first three days when most esters form. Then let it warm a little to finish. Afterwards, chill the finished beer as cold as you can for as long as you can. Even a week in the bottom of a fridge or cooler box with ice improves clarity and smoothness.

For cold storage without electricity, a pot-in-pot (zeer) cooler, two clay pots nested with wet sand between them, can lower temperatures a few degrees in dry climates. It does less in humid air.

Keep the grist simple: pilsner malt with perhaps ten to twenty per cent rice or flaked maize for lightness. Leave out crystal malt. Use soft water, with a little calcium. Choose noble-type hops with low bitterness. Mash at 64 to 66 °C for a dry finish. A simple, dry, lightly hopped beer hides nothing, so every step must be tidy.

For more on how water shapes pale beers, see brewery water from desalination.
A simple schedule and what to expect

Here is a schedule you can follow for a 20 L batch of lager-style beer with a clean ale or a warm-tolerant lager yeast:

  1. Chill the wort in an ice bath to 18 °C or below. Be patient: this may take an hour.
  2. Pitch a generous amount of yeast and aerate.
  3. Put the fermenter in a water bath with a wet cloth and fan. Keep the beer at 16 to 19 °C for the first three days.
  4. Let it rise by 2 to 3 °C for the last few days to clear diacetyl.
  5. When the gravity is stable over two days, move the beer to the coldest place you have for as long as you can wait.
  6. Prime and bottle, or keg. Then keep the beer as cold as possible.

The point of the schedule is to avoid the first-day heat spike, when yeast makes most of its flavour compounds.

Be ready for small differences. A warm-fermented lager-style beer will usually have a touch more fruitiness than a Czech or German lager and the head may be less dense. It should still be clear of butter, apple and solvent notes if you pitched well and held the temperature. If you can find a commercial lager, taste it alongside yours and note the differences in a log.

Call it what it is: a lager-style beer, or a crisp pale beer. A drinker who knows Czech pilsner will spot the difference, but may still enjoy a clean, cold pale beer on a hot afternoon. If you want to go further and make real lager, you will need cold and a conversation about equipment. We cover that in class.
faqs: Can I make real lager without a fridge?
Not really. Lager yeast needs 8 to 13 °C and weeks of cold maturation. You can make lager-style beers with a clean ale or warm-tolerant yeast.
What yeast is best for warm lager-style beer?
A clean Kölsch ale yeast, a warm-tolerant dry lager strain or a clean kveik. Pitch generously whichever you pick.
How do I cool a fermenter cheaply?
Stand it in a water bath, wrap it in a wet cloth and put a fan on it, or swap frozen bottles into the bath twice a day.
Yes. A week or more near 0 to 4 °C clears the beer and smooths the flavour, even for ale yeast beers.
